claim: Single unit activity in the OFC tracks value independent of outcome features such as identity or location or the response required to obtain the outcome.
source: Support for such pure or abstract value encoding comes largely from reports that single unit activity and the blood-oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response in the OFC tracks value, independent of outcome features such as identity or location or even the response required to obtain the outcome (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Plassmann et al., 2007; Levy and Glimcher, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies reporting value tracking in OFC.

claim: BOLD response in the OFC tracks value independent of outcome features such as identity or location or the response required to obtain the outcome.
source: Support for such pure or abstract value encoding comes largely from reports that single unit activity and the blood-oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response in the OFC tracks value, independent of outcome features such as identity or location or even the response required to obtain the outcome (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Plassmann et al., 2007; Levy and Glimcher, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies reporting value tracking in OFC.

claim: Outcome features could be the underlying basis of apparent abstract value signals in some cases.
source: Yet in some cases, outcome features could still be the underlying basis of apparent abstract value signals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative interpretations of prior findings.

claim: Some features or feature combinations might vary with value across the limited number of outcomes used in any particular session.
source: This is conceivable even if the signal correlates with value across different outcomes, since some features or feature combinations might vary with value across the limited number of outcomes used in any particular session (but see Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006, supplemental, and our correction notice).
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential confounds in prior studies.

claim: A neural element may participate in ensembles responding to more than one feature.
source: Further, any neural element (voxel or single unit) may participate in ensembles responding to more than one feature, so it is also possible that a particular element that appears not to distinguish specific features of different outcomes is in fact coding independent features that co-vary with each outcome's value.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about neural coding principles.

claim: A previously conditioned cue predicts the general value that is common to two outcomes but does not predict the unique features that distinguish the new outcome in an unblocking paradigm.
source: When this is done, the previously conditioned cue predicts the general value that is common to the two outcomes, but does not predict the unique features that distinguish the new outcome (note features are not limited to sensory properties, but might include the outcome timing, location, temperature, size, number, etc).
evidence: This is based on established learning theory principles about blocking.

claim: A target cue acquires associations with the unique features of a new outcome but not with its general or common currency value in an unblocking paradigm.
source: As a result, the target cue acquires associations with the unique features of the new outcome but not with its general or common currency value (Rescorla, 1999; Burke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating this learning principle.

claim: If OFC neurons represent only a general or common currency value, they should respond no more to a target cue than to a completely blocked cue.
source: If OFC neurons represent only a general or common currency value, divorced from features, then they should respond no more to such a target cue than to a completely blocked cue (Kamin, 1969).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on learning theory principles.

claim: If OFC neurons represent outcome features independent of value, they should respond to a target cue signaling a valueless change in outcome flavor just as they do to a cue that has been explicitly unblocked by increasing the amount of outcome delivered.
source: However, if OFC neurons represent outcome features, independent of value, then they should respond to the target cue just as they do to a cue that has been explicitly unblocked by increasing the amount of the outcome delivered.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on outcome expectancy theory.

claim: Single-unit activity was recorded in the OFC in six rats during an odor-based unblocking task.
source: We recorded single–unit activity in the OFC in six rats during an odor-based unblocking task (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Rats were trained to sample an odor in a central port following house light illumination and respond to a reward well below for two drops of Nestlé's flavored milk (chocolate or vanilla).
source: Prior to implantation with electrodes rats were trained to sample an odor in a central port following house light illumination and then respond to a reward well below for two drops of Nestlé's flavored milk (chocolate or vanilla, counterbalanced).
evidence: This describes the training procedure used in the study.

claim: Initial training was meant to establish the initial odor as a reliable predictor of a specific flavor and number of drops of milk.
source: This training was meant to establish the initial odor as a reliable predictor of a specific flavor and number of drops of milk.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the initial training phase.

claim: Each rat had extensive experience with both flavors, thus neither flavor was novel.
source: Each rat had extensive experience with both flavors, thus neither flavor was novel.
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the experimental design to control for novelty effects.

claim: Each rat underwent 7–9 rounds of unblocking after recovery from surgery and retraining.
source: When recovered from surgery, rats were retrained on the initial odor; after retraining, each rat underwent 7–9 rounds of unblocking.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: On blocked trials, the novel odor was followed by the expected two drops of the same flavor used in initial training.
source: On 'blocked' trials, the novel odor was followed by the expected two drops of the same flavor used in initial training.
evidence: This describes the blocked trial condition in the experiment.

claim: The outcome on blocked trials is fully predicted by the initial odor, thus the novel odor should be blocked from acquiring associative significance.
source: This outcome is fully predicted by the initial odor, thus the novel odor should be blocked from acquiring associative significance (Kamin, 1969).
evidence: This is based on established blocking theory, supported by citation.

claim: On flavor trials, the novel odor was followed by two drops of the flavor not used in initial training.
source: On 'flavor' trials, the novel odor was followed by two drops of the flavor not used in initial training (i.e., chocolate or vanilla).
evidence: This describes the flavor trial condition in the experiment.

claim: On flavor trials, the value is unchanged since the two flavors are equally preferred and the same amount is delivered, but the features of the outcome are different.
source: Here the value is unchanged, since the two flavors are equally preferred and the same amount is delivered, but the features of the outcome are different.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and preference testing.

claim: On flavor trials, the novel target odor should enter into associations with the unique features of the outcome.
source: Thus the novel target odor should enter into associations with the unique features of the outcome (Rescorla, 1999; Burke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a prediction based on learning theory, supported by citations.

claim: On number trials, the novel odor was followed by an additional drop of the flavor used in the initial training.
source: On 'number' trials, the novel odor was followed by an additional drop of the flavor used in the initial training.
evidence: This describes the number trial condition in the experiment.

claim: On number trials, the novel odor should enter into associations with both the features and the additional value of the outcome presented in the third drop.
source: Since the initial odor does not predict anything after the second drop, the novel odor should enter into associations with both the features and the additional value of the outcome presented in the third drop (Holland, 1984).
evidence: This is a prediction based on learning theory, supported by citation.

claim: Both chocolate and vanilla flavored milk were significantly and equally preferred to water.
source: (B) 10-min consumption testing between chocolate and water, and vanilla and water on non-training days found that both were significantly and equally preferred to water (ANOVA, F1,5 > 5, p's < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of consumption data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: No flavor preference was found between chocolate and vanilla in 2-min preference testing immediately following unblocking sessions.
source: (C) 2-min preference testing between chocolate and vanilla immediately following unblocking sessions found no flavor preference (t test, p > 0.1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of preference data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Selective devaluation of one flavor resulted in a significant difference in consumption between the non-devalued and devalued flavors.
source: (D) 20-min consumption testing from a separate group of rats (n = 8) that received selective devaluation of one of the flavors found a significant difference in consumption between the non-devalued (Con) and devalued (Dev) flavors (t test, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of consumption data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Every rat tested showed reduced consumption of the devalued flavor compared to the non-devalued flavor.
source: (D) 20-min consumption testing from a separate group of rats (n = 8) that received selective devaluation of one of the flavors found a significant difference in consumption between the non-devalued (Con) and devalued (Dev) flavors (t test, p < 0.01). This was true for every rat tested (right).
evidence: Supported by individual rat data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rats spent significantly more time in the reward well following number and flavor odors compared to blocked odors on the first three trials of the probe test.
source: (E) Time in the reward well is plotted for the probe test trials. ANOVA for time spent in the reward well with odor (blocked, number and flavor) and trial (1-15) as factors found a significant odor x trial interaction (F1,47 = 3.45, p < 0.05). Planned comparisons confirmed that on the first three trials rats spent significantly more time in the reward well following number and flavor odors compared to blocked (p's < 0.05) but responding to number and flavor did not differ (p > 0.1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Responding to number and flavor odors did not differ on the first three trials of the probe test.
source: (E) Time in the reward well is plotted for the probe test trials. ANOVA for time spent in the reward well with odor (blocked, number and flavor) and trial (1-15) as factors found a significant odor x trial interaction (F1,47 = 3.45, p < 0.05). Planned comparisons confirmed that on the first three trials rats spent significantly more time in the reward well following number and flavor odors compared to blocked (p's < 0.05) but responding to number and flavor did not differ (p > 0.1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Single unit activity was recorded from the lateral orbital and agranular insular cortices at roughly 3.2 mm anterior to bregma.
source: (F) Single unit activity was recorded from the lateral orbital and agranular insular cortices at roughly 3.2 mm anterior to bregma.
evidence: This describes the recording location, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Rats were sensitive to presentation of the novel odors, exhibiting longer latencies to respond at the reward well following odor sampling on the three novel odor trial types.
source: In the unblocking sessions rats were sensitive to presentation of the novel odors, exhibiting longer latencies to respond at the reward well following odor sampling on these three trial types.
evidence: This describes a behavioral observation from the experiment.

claim: Longer latencies to the novel odors were most apparent on the very first trial of each session, particularly on day 1.
source: Longer latencies to the novel odors were most apparent on the very first trial of each session, particularly on day 1. In support, ANOVA revealed a main effect of trial (F1,47 > 2, p's < 0.01) and a trial × day interaction (F1,47 = 34.73, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral latency data.

claim: Rats learned that the two novel odors that predicted changes in the outcome were meaningful, as evidenced by spending more time in the fluid well following sampling of the flavor and number odors than following the blocked odor in the extinction probe test.
source: However the rats also learned that the two novel odors that predicted changes in the outcome were meaningful. This was evident in the extinction probe test in which they initially spent more time in the fluid well following sampling of the flavor and number odors than following the blocked odor (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 240 single units were recorded during the first day of unblocking.
source: We recorded 240 single units during the first day of unblocking and 220 units on the second unblocking day in 48 rounds of training across all six rats (Figure 1F).
evidence: This describes the number of neurons recorded in the experiment.

claim: 220 single units were recorded on the second unblocking day.
source: We recorded 240 single units during the first day of unblocking and 220 units on the second unblocking day in 48 rounds of training across all six rats (Figure 1F).
evidence: This describes the number of neurons recorded in the experiment.

claim: 135 units showed a significant increase in firing to at least one of the odor cues.
source: This screen found 135 units (Day 1 = 79, Day 2 = 56) that showed a significant increase in firing to at least one of the odor cues.
evidence: Supported by statistical screening of neural data using t-tests.

claim: 73% of the odor-responsive neurons (98/135) exhibited activity that fell into one of two major categories.
source: The majority–98/135 or 73% of the neurons within this population–exhibited activity that fell into one of two categories (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for analysis of other neurons).
evidence: This describes the classification of recorded neurons based on their response patterns.

claim: 55 out of 135 odor-responsive neurons showed a significant phasic response to each of the four odor cues.
source: The first major category, not directly anticipated by our hypothesis, consisted of neurons (55/135, Figure 2A) that showed a significant phasic response to each of the four odor cues.
evidence: This describes the first category of neurons identified in the study.

claim: Neurons that fired to all four odors cannot be easily explained as signaling information about the predicted outcomes.
source: Since these neurons fired to all of the odors, even the blocked odor, their firing cannot be easily explained as signaling information about the predicted outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the response pattern of these neurons.

claim: Neurons that fired to all four odors might be signaling information about the cues themselves, such as their shared sensory features or intrinsic salience.
source: However they might be signaling information about the cues themselves, such as their shared sensory features or intrinsic salience.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the neural response pattern.

claim: Salience should be higher for the novel cues than for the pre-trained, initial odor, and this pattern should be most noticeable early in training when the novel cues were first presented.
source: Unlike shared sensory features, salience should be higher for the novel cues than for the pre-trained, initial odor in our design, and this pattern should be most noticeable early in training when the novel cues were first presented.
evidence: This is a prediction based on salience theory.

claim: Putative salience neurons showed greater activity to the blocked, number and flavor odors than to the more familiar, initial odor.
source: As a population, these neurons did show greater activity to the blocked, number and flavor odors than to the more familiar, initial odor (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by neural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Many putative salience neurons exhibited significantly higher firing to the novel odors than to the initial odor.
source: Further analyses of the individual units showed that many exhibited significantly higher firing to the novel odors than to the initial odor (Figure 2C), and few exhibited differences in firing among the three novel odors (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by single unit analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Few putative salience neurons exhibited differences in firing among the three novel odors.
source: Further analyses of the individual units showed that many exhibited significantly higher firing to the novel odors than to the initial odor (Figure 2C), and few exhibited differences in firing among the three novel odors (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by single unit analysis shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Activity in the putative salience population was maximal at the onset of the novel odors on the first exposure and then declined rapidly on subsequent trials.
source: Moreover, when we examined the firing of neurons in this population on the first 10 trials of unblocking (31/79 odor-responsive neurons; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), analyzing the difference in firing between the novel and initial odor cues in a sliding, 300-ms window across each trial, we found that activity in this population was maximal at the onset of the novel odors and on the first exposure and then declined rapidly on subsequent trials (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis of neural activity shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The pattern of maximal activity at novel odor onset on first exposure that declined rapidly on subsequent trials held when each novel odor was analyzed separately.
source: This same pattern held when each novel odor was analyzed separately (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by separate analysis of each odor type shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pattern of maximal activity at novel odor onset on first exposure was only seen on the first day of unblocking.
source: Further, this pattern was only seen on the first day of unblocking (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by day-specific analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The pattern of activity in putative salience neurons is consistent with signaling of the salience of the cues.
source: This pattern of activity is consistent with signaling of the salience of these cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural data based on the observed response patterns.

claim: 43 out of 135 odor-responsive neurons showed a significant phasic response to the flavor and/or number odors but did not fire to all four odors.
source: The second major category, of greater relevance to our hypothesis, consisted of neurons (43/135, Figure 3A–C) that showed a significant phasic response the flavor and/or number odors (but did not fire to all four odors).
evidence: This describes the second category of neurons identified in the study.

claim: Activity in the putative predictive neuron population was greater in response to the two predictive odor cues than to either the blocked or initial odors.
source: Activity across this population was greater in response to the two predictive odor cues than to either the blocked or initial odors (Figure 3D), and an analysis of individual units showed that nearly all of these neurons (38/43) fired more to the predictive odors than to the blocked one (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by population analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nearly all putative predictive neurons (38/43) fired more to the predictive odors than to the blocked odor.
source: Activity across this population was greater in response to the two predictive odor cues than to either the blocked or initial odors (Figure 3D), and an analysis of individual units showed that nearly all of these neurons (38/43) fired more to the predictive odors than to the blocked one (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by single unit analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The differential firing of putative predictive neurons to predictive vs blocked odors marks these neurons as candidates for encoding of associative information or meaning.
source: This result marks these neurons as candidates for encoding of associative information or meaning, since this is the primary feature that distinguishes the two odor cues from the blocked odor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural data based on the response pattern.

claim: Putative predictive neurons did not appear to distinguish, at least as a population, between the flavor and number odors.
source: Interestingly, these neurons did not appear to distinguish, at least as a population, between the flavor and number odors.
evidence: This is an observation from the neural data analysis.

claim: Putative predictive neurons showed similar levels of activity in response to both the flavor and the number odor.
source: For example, they showed similar levels of activity in response to both the flavor and the number odor (Figure 3D,F), and when we examined the firing of neurons in this population on the first 10 trials of unblocking (25/79 odor-responsive neurons, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found that differential firing to each cue developed at a similar rate during training (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: Supported by neural data shown in Figures 3D and 3F.

claim: Differential firing to the flavor and number odors developed at a similar rate during training in putative predictive neurons.
source: For example, they showed similar levels of activity in response to both the flavor and the number odor (Figure 3D,F), and when we examined the firing of neurons in this population on the first 10 trials of unblocking (25/79 odor-responsive neurons, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we found that differential firing to each cue developed at a similar rate during training (Figure 3G–J).
evidence: Supported by temporal analysis shown in Figures 3G-J.

claim: The acquisition of differential firing to the flavor and number odors demonstrates that selective odor encoding was not driven by physical properties of the odors.
source: The acquisition of differential firing to the flavor and number odors demonstrates that selective odor encoding was not driven by physical properties of the odors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal development of neural responses.

claim: If neurons were encoding the odor itself, independent of its outcome signaling, differential firing would have been apparent on the very first trial.
source: If neurons were encoding the odor itself, independent of its outcome signaling, this would have been apparent on the very first trial.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what would be expected if neurons encoded sensory properties.

claim: Putative predictive neurons responded more strongly to the unblocked 'flavor' and 'number' odors than to the 'blocked' odor.
source: Thus, as a population, these neurons responded more strongly to the unblocked 'flavor' and 'number' odors than to the 'blocked' odor.
evidence: This summarizes the key finding about the predictive neuron population.

claim: The population of putative predictive neurons responded similarly to a cue signaling a valueless change in the outcome flavor as they did to a cue signaling that more of the outcome would be delivered.
source: Even more striking, the population responded similarly to a cue signaling a valueless change in the outcome flavor as they did to a cue that signaling that more of the outcome would be delivered.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding about the equivalence of responses to flavor and number cues.

claim: Similar numbers of neurons fired to the flavor and number cues (flavor: 31, number: 37).
source: Similar numbers of neurons fired to the flavor and number cues (flavor: 31, number: 37; χ2 = 0.3, p = 0.47).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of neuron counts.

claim: Firing to the flavor cue cannot be readily explained as signaling general or common value.
source: In our design, firing to the flavor cue cannot be readily explained as signaling general or common value.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design where flavor cues signal no value change.

claim: Many OFC neurons signal associative meaning independent of at least a general value.
source: Thus these data confirm that many OFC neurons signal associative meaning independent of at least a general value.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data showing responses to valueless flavor cues.

claim: Odor firing in the flavor population was positively correlated with firing to the actual outcome delivered on flavor trials.
source: In support of this, odor firing in the flavor population, as well as the number population, was positively correlated with firing to the actual outcome delivered on each of these trials (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Odor firing in the number population was positively correlated with firing to the actual outcome delivered on number trials.
source: In support of this, odor firing in the flavor population, as well as the number population, was positively correlated with firing to the actual outcome delivered on each of these trials (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The relationship between odor and outcome firing supports the idea that cue-evoked activity in the flavor population is signaling features of the new outcome.
source: This relationship supports the idea that cue-evoked activity in the flavor population is signaling features of the new outcome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between cue and outcome firing.

claim: Greater selective firing to the flavor odor was associated with greater selective firing to the flavor outcome (R2 = 0.41, p < 0.01).
source: (A) For each predictive neuron that significantly increased firing to the flavor odor (total n = 31; flavor-only n = 6 [green]; number and flavor n = 24 [purple]) we plotted its selective firing to the flavor odor (x-axis; [normalized flavor odor firing – mean(normalized initial odor firing, normalized blocked odor firing, normalized number odor firing)]) against its selective firing to the flavor outcome (y-axis; [normalized flavor outcome firing – mean(normalized initial outcome firing, normalized blocked outcome firing, normalized number outcome firing)]). Comparison of odor firing of single neurons to the population found a single outlier (neuron firing was 3 stdev > population firing). The outlier was omitted from this analysis. There was a significant, positive relationship such that greater selective firing to the flavor odor was associated with greater selective firing the flavor outcome (R2 = 0.41, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was zero correlation between selective flavor odor firing and selective number outcome firing (R2 = 0.01, p = 0.70).
source: (B) This relationship was restricted to the flavor outcome; plotting selective flavor odor firing against selective number outcome firing revealed zero correlation (R2 = 0.01, p = 0.70; calculation identical to A only mean(blocked, initial and flavor outcome firing) was subtracted from number outcome firing.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Greater selective firing to the number odor was associated with greater selective firing to the number outcome (R2 = 0.27, p < 0.01).
source: (C) For each predictive neuron that significantly increased firing to the number odor (total n = 37; number only n = 12 [blue]; number and flavor n = 23 [purple]) we plotted it's selective firing to the number odor (x-axis; [normalized number odor firing – mean(normalized initial odor firing, normalized blocked odor firing, normalized flavor odor firing)]) against its selective firing to the number outcome (y-axis; [normalized number outcome firing – mean(normalized initial outcome firing, normalized blocked outcome firing, normalized flavor outcome firing)]). Two neurons showed selective odor firing 3 stdev above the population mean and were excluded from analysis. There was a significant, positive relationship such that greater selective firing to the number odor was associated with greater selective firing the number outcome (R2 = 0.27, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was zero correlation between selective number odor firing and selective flavor outcome firing (R2 = 0.04, p = 0.26).
source: (D) This relationship was restricted to the number outcome; plotting selective number odor firing against selective flavor outcome firing revealed zero correlation (R2 = 0.04, p = 0.26) calculation identical to C only mean(blocked, initial and number outcome firing) was subtracted from flavor outcome firing.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The unblocking procedure revealed two distinct populations of OFC neurons.
source: This approach revealed two distinct populations of OFC neurons.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding of the study.

claim: One population of OFC neurons fired immediately on initial presentation of all three target cues, perhaps reflecting these cues' novelty or salience.
source: One population consisted of neurons that fired immediately on initial presentation of all three target cues, perhaps reflecting these cues' novelty or salience.
evidence: This summarizes the characteristics of the first population identified.

claim: The finding of neural correlates of salience in OFC is consistent with prior reports.
source: While unexpected and not directly relevant to the question motivating this study, this finding is consistent with reports of neural correlates of salience in OFC (Kahnt and Tobler, 2013; Ogawa et al., 2013) and with studies implicating the OFC in phenomena such as latent inhibition, set formation, and even auto-shaping (Chudasama et al., 2003; Schiller and Weiner, 2004; Chase et al., 2012) which depend in part on the appropriate attribution of salience to cues.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on OFC and salience.

claim: Studies have implicated the OFC in phenomena such as latent inhibition, set formation, and auto-shaping which depend in part on the appropriate attribution of salience to cues.
source: While unexpected and not directly relevant to the question motivating this study, this finding is consistent with reports of neural correlates of salience in OFC (Kahnt and Tobler, 2013; Ogawa et al., 2013) and with studies implicating the OFC in phenomena such as latent inhibition, set formation, and even auto-shaping (Chudasama et al., 2003; Schiller and Weiner, 2004; Chase et al., 2012) which depend in part on the appropriate attribution of salience to cues.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on OFC function.

claim: These results point to a largely unappreciated role for OFC in the modulation of attention for the purposes of learning.
source: Together these results point to a largely unappreciated role for this area in the modulation of attention for the purposes of learning (Esber et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Modern learning theories describe salience as a function of both intrinsic and acquired properties.
source: Modern learning theories describe salience as a function of both intrinsic and acquired properties.
evidence: This is based on established learning theory.

claim: The putative salience population was correlated with intrinsic salience.
source: Within this framework, this population was correlated with intrinsic salience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural data in the context of learning theory.

claim: The second population of neurons fired preferentially to the target cues that predicted changes in the outcome flavor.
source: The second population, of more direct relevance to our hypothesis, consisted of neurons that fired preferentially to the target cues that predicted changes in the outcome flavor.
evidence: This summarizes the characteristics of the second population identified.

claim: Nearly all neurons in the second population fired more to predictive cues than to the similarly trained but fully blocked cue.
source: Nearly all of these neurons fired more to these cues than to the similarly trained but fully blocked cue, and this activity was acquired with learning, a pattern consistent with signaling of the associative significance or meaning of these cues (or possibly their acquired salience).
evidence: This describes the response pattern of the second population.

claim: Activity in the second population was acquired with learning, a pattern consistent with signaling of the associative significance or meaning of these cues.
source: Nearly all of these neurons fired more to these cues than to the similarly trained but fully blocked cue, and this activity was acquired with learning, a pattern consistent with signaling of the associative significance or meaning of these cues (or possibly their acquired salience).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal development of neural responses.

claim: The acquired neural activity was observed to both the explicitly unblocked 'number' cue as well as to the 'flavor' cue.
source: Importantly, the acquired neural activity was observed to both the explicitly unblocked 'number' cue as well as to the 'flavor' cue, which was unblocked by shifting the features of the expected outcome while holding the value constant.
evidence: This describes a key finding about responses to both types of unblocked cues.

claim: The flavor cue was unblocked by shifting the features of the expected outcome while holding the value constant.
source: Importantly, the acquired neural activity was observed to both the explicitly unblocked 'number' cue as well as to the 'flavor' cue, which was unblocked by shifting the features of the expected outcome while holding the value constant.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation for the flavor condition.

claim: The lack of any flavor preference makes it unlikely that the cue added prior to the flavor manipulation acquired what might be termed a general or cached value.
source: The lack of any flavor preference makes it unlikely that the cue added prior to this manipulation acquired what might be termed a general or cached value.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preference testing data.

claim: Responding to the flavor target cue in the probe test is dissociable from even the smallest animal-by-animal differences in conditioned or unconditioned responding to the two outcomes used.
source: Indeed, in prior work we have found that responding to this target cue in the probe test is dissociable from even the smallest animal-by-animal differences in conditioned or unconditioned responding to the two outcomes used (Schoenbaum et al., 2011), indicating that it is not driven by any sort of shift in value that might accrue to the cue.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Responding to the flavor target cue is not driven by any sort of shift in value that might accrue to the cue.
source: Indeed, in prior work we have found that responding to this target cue in the probe test is dissociable from even the smallest animal-by-animal differences in conditioned or unconditioned responding to the two outcomes used (Schoenbaum et al., 2011), indicating that it is not driven by any sort of shift in value that might accrue to the cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings, supported by citation.

claim: Conditioned responding to a target cue unblocked by shifting the identity of the outcome seems to be particularly dependent upon the unexpected outcome's unique features.
source: Instead conditioned responding to a target cue unblocked by shifting the identity of the outcome seems to be particularly dependent upon the unexpected outcome's unique features, at least in comparison to an explicitly unblocked cue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and learning theory.

claim: Conditioned reinforcement supported by a normally trained cue is insensitive to devaluation of the predicted outcome.
source: For example, conditioned reinforcement supported by a normally trained cue is insensitive to devaluation of the predicted outcome (Parkinson et al., 2005); however if the cue is trained like the 'flavor' cue in the current experiment, then devaluation of the predicted outcome completely abolishes the ability of the cue to serve as a conditioned reinforcer (Burke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: If a cue is trained like the 'flavor' cue in the current experiment, then devaluation of the predicted outcome completely abolishes the ability of the cue to serve as a conditioned reinforcer.
source: For example, conditioned reinforcement supported by a normally trained cue is insensitive to devaluation of the predicted outcome (Parkinson et al., 2005); however if the cue is trained like the 'flavor' cue in the current experiment, then devaluation of the predicted outcome completely abolishes the ability of the cue to serve as a conditioned reinforcer (Burke et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A cue trained like the flavor cue has little or no intrinsic, cached or acquired value except what can be inferred through knowledge of the features of the outcome.
source: This result indicates that a cue trained in this manner has little or no intrinsic, cached or acquired value except what can be inferred through knowledge of the features of the outcome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the devaluation findings cited.

claim: Cues trained like the flavor cue retain the ability to support Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer when that transfer is specific to the outcome.
source: This cue's special link to the sensory features of the outcome is also apparent in that such cues retain the ability to support Pavlovian-to-instrumental transfer when that transfer is specific to the outcome (Rescorla, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Outcome-specific transfer is insensitive to devaluation.
source: Interestingly outcome-specific transfer is both insensitive to devaluation (Holland, 2004) and disrupted by OFC lesions (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), results which are difficult to reconcile with the view that the OFC is directly involved in the representation of value.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Outcome-specific transfer is disrupted by OFC lesions.
source: Interestingly outcome-specific transfer is both insensitive to devaluation (Holland, 2004) and disrupted by OFC lesions (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), results which are difficult to reconcile with the view that the OFC is directly involved in the representation of value.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The insensitivity of outcome-specific transfer to devaluation and its disruption by OFC lesions are difficult to reconcile with the view that the OFC is directly involved in the representation of value.
source: Interestingly outcome-specific transfer is both insensitive to devaluation (Holland, 2004) and disrupted by OFC lesions (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), results which are difficult to reconcile with the view that the OFC is directly involved in the representation of value.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings.

claim: OFC neurons developed robust responses to a valueless cue.
source: That OFC neurons developed robust responses to such a valueless cue indicates that many OFC neurons—more than half of the population responsive to the acquired significance of the cues—represent associative features that must be, strictly speaking, independent of general or common value.
evidence: This summarizes a key finding of the study.

claim: More than half of the population of OFC neurons responsive to the acquired significance of cues represent associative features that are independent of general or common value.
source: That OFC neurons developed robust responses to such a valueless cue indicates that many OFC neurons—more than half of the population responsive to the acquired significance of the cues—represent associative features that must be, strictly speaking, independent of general or common value.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data.

claim: The predictive population included neurons that fired only to the flavor cue as well as neurons that participated in both the flavor and number ensembles.
source: Notably this population included neurons that fired only to the flavor cue as well as neurons that participated in both the flavor and number ensembles.
evidence: This describes the composition of the predictive neuron population.

claim: Dual encoding of flavor and number would be expected if individual neurons participate in ensembles coding more than one outcome feature.
source: Such dual encoding would be expected if, as suggested earlier, individual neurons are not labeled lines but participate in ensembles coding more than one outcome feature (flavor, number, temperature, location, timing, etc).
evidence: This is an inference based on neural coding principles.

claim: Some neurons fired preferentially to the valued, number cue.
source: Of course some neurons fired preferentially to the valued, number cue.
evidence: This describes a subset of the neural responses observed.

claim: The firing of neurons preferentially responsive to the number cue could reflect the general value that accrued to this cue during training.
source: The firing of these neurons could reflect the general value that accrued to this cue during training.
evidence: This is one possible interpretation of the neural data.

claim: The firing of neurons preferentially responsive to the number cue could equally well reflect associations with features of the additional outcome delivered on these trials.
source: However such firing could equally well reflect associations with features of the additional outcome delivered on these trials, known to develop when additional rewards are delivered during unblocking (Holland, 1984).
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Associations with features of additional outcomes are known to develop when additional rewards are delivered during unblocking.
source: However such firing could equally well reflect associations with features of the additional outcome delivered on these trials, known to develop when additional rewards are delivered during unblocking (Holland, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The similarities in the overall level of neural activity to the flavor and number cues, their similar rates of development with learning, and the finding that neurons develop activity to a valueless cue make the feature-based explanation the most parsimonious.
source: While it is impossible to say for sure, the similarities in the overall level of neural activity to the flavor and number cues, their similar rates of development with learning, and the finding that neurons do develop activity to a valueless cue make the latter explanation the most parsimonious.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of neural data.

claim: If OFC neurons signal associations between cues and specific outcome features, this would accord well with results showing that the OFC is not necessary when behavior or learning can be accomplished using general value alone.
source: If OFC neurons signal associations between cues and specific outcome features, this would accord well with results showing that the OFC is not necessary when behavior—or learning—can be accomplished using general value alone.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior literature.

claim: The OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: The OFC is not required for discrimination learning.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: The OFC is not required for extinction by reward omission.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior lesion study.

claim: The OFC is not required for transfer.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior lesion study.

claim: The OFC may not be required for reversal learning.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior lesion study, though stated with some uncertainty.

claim: Simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning, discrimination learning, extinction by reward omission, transfer, and reversal learning can all be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
source: For example, the OFC is not required for simple Pavlovian or instrumental conditioning (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; Gremel and Costa, 2013) discrimination learning (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Walton et al., 2010), extinction by reward omission (Takahashi et al., 2009), transfer (Ostlund and Balleine, 2007), and even perhaps reversal learning (Rudebeck et al., 2013), all of which can be accomplished without reference to specific information about predicted outcomes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about these learning processes.

claim: Both blocking and unblocking (when it can be accounted for by value) do not require the OFC.
source: Similarly both blocking and unblocking—when it can be accounted for by value—do not require the OFC (Burke et al., 2008; McDannald et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior lesion studies.

claim: Preserved function after OFC lesions could reflect compensation by other areas.
source: While the preserved function in these studies could reflect compensation by other areas, it must at least call into question the idea that OFC, writ large, is fundamental to all behavior that reflects value, instead highlighting suggestions that common value representation may at least be limited to the medial subregion (Noonan et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of lesion study findings.

claim: Common value representation in OFC may be limited to the medial subregion.
source: While the preserved function in these studies could reflect compensation by other areas, it must at least call into question the idea that OFC, writ large, is fundamental to all behavior that reflects value, instead highlighting suggestions that common value representation may at least be limited to the medial subregion (Noonan et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Recent work in humans has shown that OFC represents specific outcome features.
source: Indeed recent work in humans has shown that OFC represents specific outcome features and that more lateral orbital areas represent those outcomes in a way that is dependent upon prior cues (Klein-Flugge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent human neuroimaging work.

claim: More lateral orbital areas represent outcomes in a way that is dependent upon prior cues.
source: Indeed recent work in humans has shown that OFC represents specific outcome features and that more lateral orbital areas represent those outcomes in a way that is dependent upon prior cues (Klein-Flugge et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent human neuroimaging work.

claim: Far from signaling general value about outcomes without regard to their features and attendant events, the OFC maintains highly specific representations.
source: Thus far from signaling general value about outcomes without regard to their features and attendant events, this work shows that the OFC maintains highly specific representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and cited work.

claim: Highly specific representations in OFC are consistent with observations that the OFC is necessary for behaviors that require knowledge of outcome features to recognize errors or to derive or infer a value.
source: Such highly specific representations are consistent with observations that the OFC is necessary for superficially similar behaviors (Pavlovian or instrumental responding, discriminations, even learning) when they require knowledge of the outcome features in order to recognize errors or to derive or infer a value (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Ostlund and Balleine, 2007; McDannald et al., 2011; Gremel and Costa, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior lesion studies, supported by citations.

claim: The OFC is required for the development of conditioned responding to the target cue paired with a shift in outcome identity but not to the target cue paired with additional outcome.
source: This is even true in the current paradigm, where we have shown that the OFC is required for the development of conditioned responding to the target cue paired with a shift in outcome identity but not to the target cue paired with additional outcome (McDannald et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior lesion work using the same paradigm.

claim: The finding of robust encoding of a valueless Pavlovian cue that exceeds that of a blocked cue and is equivalent to a cue paired with additional outcome provides further support for outcome expectancy theories of OFC function.
source: Our present finding of robust encoding of a valueless Pavlovian cue that exceeds that of a blocked cue, and is equivalent to a cue paired with additional outcome, provides further support for outcome expectancy theories of OFC function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neural data.

claim: Male Long-Evans rats were obtained at 200–250 g from Charles River Labs.
source: Male Long-Evans rats were obtained at 200–250 g from Charles River Labs, (Wilmington, MA).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Rats were tested at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and the NIDA-IRP in accordance with SOM and NIH guidelines.
source: Rats were tested at the University of Maryland School of Medicine and the NIDA-IRP in accordance with SOM and NIH guidelines (12-CNRB-108).
evidence: This describes the institutional approval and ethical guidelines followed.

claim: A drivable bundle of 16, 25 µm diameter FeNiCr wires was chronically implanted dorsal to OFC in the left hemisphere at 3.0 mm anterior to bregma, 3.2 mm laterally, and 4.0 mm ventral to the surface of the brain.
source: Using aseptic, stereotaxic surgical techniques, a drivable bundle of 16, 25 µm diameter FeNiCr wires (Stablohm 675, California Fine Wire, Grover Beach, CA) was chronically implanted dorsal to OFC in the left hemisphere at 3.0 mm anterior to bregma, 3.2 mm laterally, and 4.0 mm ventral to the surface of the brain in each rat.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for electrode implantation.

claim: Electrodes were electroplated with platinum to an impedance of ∼300 kΩ immediately prior to implantation.
source: Immediately prior to implantation, these wires were freshly cut with surgical scissors to extend ∼1 mm beyond the cannula and electroplated with platinum (H2PtCl6; Aldrich, Milwaukee, WI) to an impedance of ∼300 kΩ.
evidence: This describes the electrode preparation procedure.

claim: The final electrode position was marked by passing a 15 µA current through each electrode at the end of the study.
source: At the end of the study, the final electrode position was marked by passing a 15 µA current through each electrode.
evidence: This describes the histological verification procedure.

claim: Rats were water deprived by restricting daily access to 1 hr following each training session prior to implantation with microelectrodes.
source: Prior to implantation with microelectrodes, rats were water deprived by restricting daily access to 1 hr following each training session.
evidence: This describes the water restriction procedure used for training.

claim: Water-deprived rats were progressively shaped to hold in the odor port for 1 s to receive two drops of water at the well.
source: Water-deprived rats were progressively shaped to hold in the odor port for 1 s to receive two drops of water at the well.
evidence: This describes the initial shaping procedure.

claim: After shaping, rats received further training until they were proficiently responding for the initial odor in order to receive two boli of milk (vanilla or chocolate-flavored, counterbalanced).
source: After shaping, rats received further training until they were proficiently responding for the initial odor in order to receive two boli of milk (vanilla or chocolate-flavored, counterbalanced); this involved as many as 15 sessions, with a maximum of 240 trials in each session.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Proficient responding was characterized as correctly completing ∼200 trials per session.
source: Proficient responding was characterized as correctly completing ∼200 trials per session.
evidence: This defines the criterion for proficient performance.

claim: On alternate days during training, rats were given 20-min ad libitum exposure to the untrained milk flavor.
source: On alternate days, rats were given 20-min ad libitum exposure to the untrained milk flavor.
evidence: This describes the exposure procedure to ensure familiarity with both flavors.

claim: Rats completed between 30–60 trials involving each novel odor per session during unblocking.
source: Rats completed between 30–60 trials involving each novel odor per session.
evidence: This describes the trial structure during unblocking sessions.

claim: On the probe test day, rats received a brief reminder of each trial type (∼10 total trials) and then were presented the novel odors alone without reward.
source: On the subsequent probe test day, rats received a brief reminder of each trial type, ∼10 total trials and then were presented the novel odors alone without reward, interleaved with trials in which the initial odor was presented with reward, in order to maintain responding.
evidence: This describes the probe test procedure.

claim: On unrewarded, novel-odor extinction trials during the probe test, the requirement to sample the odor for 1-s and respond to the reward well was lifted.
source: On the unrewarded, novel-odor extinction trials, the requirement to sample the odor for 1-s and respond to the reward well was lifted.
evidence: This describes the modified trial structure for probe test extinction trials.

claim: The unblocking procedure was repeated seven to nine times per rat using a new set of blocked, number and flavor odors each time.
source: The unblocking procedure was repeated seven to nine times per rat using a new set of blocked, number and flavor odors each time; in some cases, a new initial odor was also trained prior to repeating unblocking.
evidence: This describes the repeated testing procedure.

claim: When the initial odor was changed, rats were trained on the new initial odor for 4–5 sessions prior to the first unblocking procedure with that odor.
source: When the initial odor was changed rats were trained on the new initial odor for 4–5 sessions prior to the first unblocking procedure with that odor.
evidence: This describes the retraining procedure when initial odors were changed.

claim: Consumption tests were given in a housing cage separate from the home cage and experimental chamber.
source: Consumption tests were given in a housing cage separate from their home cage and experimental chamber.
evidence: This describes the setting for consumption tests.

claim: 10-min consumption tests comparing one flavored milk to water occurred on days when unblocking training was not performed.
source: In the first, consumption of one of the flavored milks (chocolate or vanilla) was compared to consumption of water. These tests were 10-min in duration and occurred on days when unblocking training was not performed.
evidence: This describes the first type of consumption test.

claim: 2-min consumption tests directly comparing the two flavored milks occurred immediately following unblocking sessions.
source: The second test directly compared consumption of the two flavored milks. These tests were 2-min in duration and occurred immediately following unblocking sessions.
evidence: This describes the second type of consumption test.

claim: The 2-min consumption tests immediately following unblocking sessions were critical for showing that rats did not become selectively sated to the flavored milk they experienced more in the unblocking sessions.
source: This second test was critical for showing that rats did not become selectively sated to the flavored milk they experienced more in the unblocking sessions.
evidence: This explains the purpose of the immediate post-session consumption test.

claim: For all consumption tests, the location of the bottles was swapped roughly every 20–30 s to equate time on each side.
source: For all tests the location of the bottles was swapped roughly every 20–30 s to equate time on each side.
evidence: This describes a control procedure in the consumption tests.

claim: Naïve rats were exposed to the vanilla and chocolate-flavored milk twice each in 1-hr sessions during the selective conditioned flavor aversion procedure.
source: Naïve rats were exposed to the vanilla and chocolate-flavored milk twice each in 1-hr sessions.
evidence: This describes the pre-exposure phase of the conditioned aversion procedure.

claim: During pre-exposure sessions in the conditioned aversion procedure, intraperitoneal saline injections were given to habituate rats to the injection procedure.
source: During pre-exposure sessions intraperitoneal saline injections (0.9%, 5 ml/kg i.p.) were given to habituate rats to the injection procedure.
evidence: This describes the habituation procedure for injections.

claim: Conditioning in the selective conditioned flavor aversion procedure consisted of five, 1-hr exposures to each of the two solutions spaced over 10 days.
source: Conditioning consisted of five, 1-hr exposures to each of the two solutions spaced over 10 days.
evidence: This describes the conditioning phase of the aversion procedure.

claim: Exposure to the devalued flavor was followed by injection of lithium chloride (0.3 M LiCl, 5 ml/kg i.p.) in the conditioned aversion procedure.
source: Exposure to the devalued flavor was followed by injection of lithium chloride (0.3 M LiCl, 5 ml/kg i.p.).
evidence: This describes the devaluation procedure.

claim: Exposure to the control flavor was followed by injection of saline in the conditioned aversion procedure.
source: Exposure to the control flavor was followed by injection of saline.
evidence: This describes the control condition in the aversion procedure.

claim: All factors (identity of devalued flavor, order of flavor presentation, side of flavor during choice test) were fully counterbalanced in the conditioned aversion procedure.
source: All factors (identity of devalued flavor, order of flavor presentation, side of flavor during choice test) were fully counterbalanced.
evidence: This describes the counterbalancing in the experimental design.

claim: Neural activity was recorded using two identical Plexon Multichannel Acquisition Processor systems interfaced with odor discrimination training chambers.
source: Neural activity was recorded using two identical Plexon Multichannel Acquisition Processor systems (Dallas, TX), interfaced with odor discrimination training chambers described above.
evidence: This describes the recording equipment used.

claim: After recovery from surgery, electrodes were advanced daily until activity was obtained on a majority of wires.
source: After recovery from surgery, electrodes were advanced daily until activity was obtained on a majority of wires.
evidence: This describes the electrode positioning procedure.

claim: During electrode advancement, rats received reminder training using the pre-trained initial odor.
source: During this process, rats received reminder training using the pre-trained initial odor, as described above.
evidence: This describes the training procedure during electrode positioning.

claim: During each 3-day unblocking procedure, the electrode was generally left in the same position.
source: During this 3-day procedure, the electrode was generally left in the same position.
evidence: This describes the electrode positioning during unblocking sessions.

claim: Following the completion of each 3-day unblocking procedure, the electrode was advanced 40–80 µm.
source: Following the completion of each 3-day unblocking procedure, the electrode was advanced 40–80 µm, and the process was repeated using new odor cues to test neurons in a new location in OFC.
evidence: This describes the electrode advancement procedure between unblocking rounds.

claim: Units were sorted using Offline Sorter software from Plexon Inc using a template matching algorithm.
source: Units were sorted using Offline Sorter software from Plexon Inc (Dallas, TX) using a template matching algorithm.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting procedure.

claim: Activity to the novel odors was examined from 300–1300 ms after initial odor onset, which corresponded approximately to the time during which the novel odors were delivered to the odor port.
source: To examine activity to the novel odors, we examined activity from 300–1300 ms after initial odor onset, which corresponded approximately to the time during which the novel odors were delivered to the odor port.
evidence: This describes the time window used for analyzing novel odor responses.

claim: Activity to the flavor outcome was examined for 2000 ms starting with the first drop delivery.
source: To examine activity to the flavor outcome, we examined activity for 2000 ms starting with the first drop delivery.
evidence: This describes the time window used for analyzing flavor outcome responses.

claim: Activity to the number outcome was examined for 2000 ms starting 1000 ms following first drop delivery, coinciding with the third drop delivery.
source: To examine activity to the number outcome, we examined activity for 2000 ms starting 1000 ms following first drop delivery, coinciding with the third drop delivery.
evidence: This describes the time window used for analyzing number outcome responses.

claim: The inter-trial interval was defined as the 2 s prior to illumination of the house light.
source: The inter-trial interval was defined as the 2 s prior to illumination of the house light.
evidence: This defines the baseline period for neural activity analysis.

claim: Normalized firing was calculated by taking the firing rate during a period of interest minus firing rate during the ITI.
source: Normalized firing was calculated by taking the firing rate during a period of interest minus firing rate during the ITI: Normalized firing = (Period spikes/s) − (ITI spikes/s).
evidence: This describes the normalization procedure for neural activity.

claim: Neurons were identified as being odor responsive with a Bonferroni-corrected t test (p < 0.0125) comparing elevations in firing during each of the four odor epochs from their respective ITIs.
source: Neurons were identified as being odor responsive with a Bonferroni-corrected t test (four separate tests, 0.05/4 = 0.0125; p < 0.0125) comparing elevations in firing during each of the four odor epochs (initial, blocked, number and flavor) from their respective ITIs.
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion for identifying odor-responsive neurons.

claim: Neurons were classified as putative salience neurons if they significantly increased firing to all odors.
source: Neurons were classified as putative salience neurons if they significantly increased firing to all odors; putative predictive neurons were classified by significantly increasing firing to either or both the number and flavor odors, but not to all four odors.
evidence: This describes the classification criterion for salience neurons.

claim: Putative predictive neurons were classified by significantly increasing firing to either or both the number and flavor odors, but not to all four odors.
source: Neurons were classified as putative salience neurons if they significantly increased firing to all odors; putative predictive neurons were classified by significantly increasing firing to either or both the number and flavor odors, but not to all four odors.
evidence: This describes the classification criterion for predictive neurons.

claim: Single-unit and population activity was plotted in 50-ms bins.
source: Single-unit and population activity was plotted in 50-ms bins; population activity was analyzed with repeated measures ANOVA with bin (50 ms) and odor trial (initial, blocked, number and flavor) as factors.
evidence: This describes the temporal binning for neural activity plots.

claim: Population activity was analyzed with repeated measures ANOVA with bin (50 ms) and odor trial (initial, blocked, number and flavor) as factors.
source: Single-unit and population activity was plotted in 50-ms bins; population activity was analyzed with repeated measures ANOVA with bin (50 ms) and odor trial (initial, blocked, number and flavor) as factors.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach for population activity.

claim: Heat plots were constructed by calculating difference scores between normalized firing in 200-ms sliding windows moving away from the novel odor onset in 50 ms increments.
source: Heat plots were constructed by calculating difference scores between normalized firing to Novel and Initial odors (Figure 2F), Number and Blocked odors (Figure 3G) and Flavor and Blocked odors, in 200-ms sliding windows moving away from the novel odor onset in 50 ms increments.
evidence: This describes the method for constructing heat plots.

claim: For purposes of visualization only, single unit and population firing, as well as heat plot comparisons were smoothed by taking a four-bin average moving in 50 ms increments.
source: Finally, for purposes of visualization only; single unit and population firing, as well as heat plot comparisons were smoothed by taking a four-bin average moving in 50 ms increments.
evidence: This describes the smoothing procedure applied for visualization.

claim: All statistical analyses were performed on unsmoothed data.
source: All statistical analyses were performed on unsmoothed data.
evidence: This clarifies that smoothing was only for visualization, not analysis.
